tracks.title: Digital confidence
tracks.summary: Start from zero. Build the habits that make every other skill easier.

missions.title: Create your first controlled workspace
missions.principle: A folder groups work; a filename identifies a file; a version records a change. An approved file can be older than an unapproved draft.
missions.example: incoming/menu.txt is unreviewed; approved/menu-v2.txt is reviewed. Keep both their version and approval state visible.

visual.caption: A folder groups work; a filename identifies a file; a version records a change.

missions.title: Share a file safely
missions.principle: Permission controls what someone may do. A named viewer can read; an editor can change. Public access is a separate decision.
missions.example: A named supplier sees order totals as a viewer. They do not receive customer phone numbers or edit permission.

visual.caption: Permission controls what someone may do.

tracks.title: Data & decision making
tracks.summary: Turn raw records into careful, explainable business decisions.

missions.title: Read a table with confidence
missions.principle: A row is one record; a column describes one attribute. An identifier distinguishes records even when names repeat.
missions.example: Order O-101 is one row. amount is one column. order_id should be unique even when two customer names match.

missions.title: Name the parts of a computer and their jobs
missions.principle: Hardware is the physical machine and software is the instructions it runs. Input, processing, memory, storage and output each do a different job.
missions.example: Typing uses the keyboard as input. The bill sits in memory while open and is written to storage when saved. The printer is the output device.

visual.caption: Hardware is the physical machine and software is the instructions it runs.

missions.principle: Priority comes from how many people are affected and how serious the effect is, not from who shouts loudest.

missions.title: Survey a site and set the purpose of each camera
missions.principle: Each camera should have a job, such as identifying a face at a door or watching a wide yard. The job decides position, lens and lighting.
missions.example: The door camera is for identifying people entering, so it is placed at face height and angled to avoid the bright glass behind them.

missions.principle: Cable length, power and connectors determine whether a camera works. Standard Ethernet has a distance limit, and power over Ethernet shares a fixed power budget.

missions.title: Calculate storage and retention
missions.principle: Storage depends on bit rate, number of cameras and days kept. Under-sizing loses footage you promised to keep.
missions.example: One camera at 4 Mbps records about 43.2 GB per day, so 8 cameras need about 346 GB per day and 10.4 TB for 30 days. An 8 TB drive is not enough.

missions.title: Estimate a sensible cost of capital
missions.principle: Debt and equity cost different amounts and the average weighted by their share is the cost of capital. Cheaper debt raises financial risk.

missions.title: Show why countries trade with comparative advantage
missions.principle: A country gains from specialising in what it produces at the lowest opportunity cost, even if another country is better at everything.
missions.example: If one country gives up less grain to produce each unit of cloth, it specialises in cloth and trades, even though the other country may be more productive overall.

missions.title: Summarise data with the right measures
missions.principle: Mean, median and mode describe the centre of data. Spread tells how far values vary. The best measure depends on the shape.
missions.example: The mean is 33.5 but the median is 21.5. The one large month pulls the mean up, so the median describes a typical month better.

missions.title: Calculate simple and conditional probability
missions.principle: Probability is the share of favourable outcomes. Conditional probability changes when new information is known.
missions.example: Faulty chance is 0.6 times 0.02 plus 0.4 times 0.05, which is 0.032. Given a fault, the chance it came from A is 0.012 divided by 0.032, about 37.5 percent.

visual.caption: Probability is the share of favourable outcomes.

missions.title: Judge a sample before trusting it
missions.principle: A sample is only useful if it represents the population. Bias in how people are chosen cannot be fixed by making the sample larger.
missions.example: Asking only customers who come to the shop on weekends misses weekday customers, so a random sample from all invoices is used instead.

visual.caption: A sample is only useful if it represents the population.

missions.title: Explain what makes something a human right
missions.principle: Human rights belong to every person because they are human. They are universal, equal and not granted by a government, though governments must respect and protect them.

visual.caption: Human rights belong to every person because they are human.

missions.title: Explain what shapes a community's health

missions.title: Apply the five laws of library science
missions.principle: The five laws put the reader first: books are for use, every reader has a book, every book has its reader, save the reader's time, and a library is a growing organism.
missions.example: Locked books that children cannot borrow break the law that books are for use, so a supervised borrowing rule is introduced.

visual.caption: The five laws put the reader first: books are for use, every reader has a book, every book has its reader, save the reader's time, and a library is a growing organism.

missions.title: Describe palmistry honestly
missions.principle: Palmistry is a traditional art of reading hands for character and life themes. There is no proof that lines predict events, so claims must be modest.

missions.title: Measure specific gravity
missions.principle: Specific gravity compares a stone's weight with water. It is calculated from weights in air and in water, and helps separate similar stones.

missions.title: Treat crystal healing claims honestly
missions.principle: Crystals are meaningful to many people, but there is no evidence they treat disease. Honest sellers describe belief as belief.

missions.title: Explain the fire triangle and why fires spread
missions.principle: Fire needs fuel, heat and oxygen, and spreads by conduction, convection and radiation. Removing one element stops the fire, and smoke is often the first danger.
missions.example: A rubbish bin fire next to a curtain shows how radiant heat ignites nearby fuel, and the briefing tells staff to leave rather than fight a spreading fire.

visual.caption: Fire needs fuel, heat and oxygen, and spreads by conduction, convection and radiation.

tracks.title: Disaster Management
tracks.summary: Plan for and respond to disasters: hazard types, risk and vulnerability, early warning, shelter and relief planning, incident command, psychosocial support, recovery and community resilience.

missions.title: Describe the disaster management cycle
missions.principle: Disaster management has phases of mitigation, preparedness, response and recovery. Each phase has its own actions, and good work in earlier phases reduces harm later.

missions.title: Classify food hazards
missions.principle: Food can be unsafe because of biological, chemical, physical or allergen hazards. Naming the hazard is the first step in controlling it.
missions.example: A piece of metal from a damaged sieve is a physical hazard, and undeclared nuts are an allergen hazard.

visual.caption: Food can be unsafe because of biological, chemical, physical or allergen hazards.

missions.title: Understand how microbes grow in food
missions.principle: Microbes need nutrients, moisture, warmth and time. The temperature danger zone is where many bacteria grow fastest.
missions.example: Three hours is nine doublings, which gives 100 times 512, or 51200, so food is kept cold or hot rather than left at room temperature.

visual.caption: Microbes need nutrients, moisture, warmth and time.

tracks.title: Security Services & Crisis Management
tracks.summary: Prepare for professional private security work: duties, legal limits, observation, access control, emergencies, communication, de-escalation, reporting and ethical conduct.

missions.title: Describe the security officer's role and limits
missions.principle: A security officer protects people and property by prevention, observation and reporting. The role does not give police powers, and the law sets strict limits.
missions.example: The statement says that the guard observes and reports and does not search residents or use force except as the law allows in self-defence.

missions.title: Use Ohm's law and power formulas
missions.principle: Voltage, current, resistance and power are linked by simple formulas. Correct calculation is the base of safe design.
missions.example: Current is 2300 divided by 230, which is 10 amps, resistance is 23 ohms and 4 hours uses 9.2 kilowatt hours.

visual.caption: Voltage, current, resistance and power are linked by simple formulas.

missions.title: Explain heat transfer and the refrigeration cycle
missions.principle: Heat moves by conduction, convection and radiation. A refrigeration cycle moves heat from a cooler space to a warmer one using a refrigerant, compressor, condenser, expansion device and evaporator.
missions.example: In the evaporator the low-pressure liquid absorbs room heat and boils to vapour, and in the condenser the hot vapour releases heat outdoors.

visual.caption: Heat moves by conduction, convection and radiation.

glossary.definition: A defined way for one program to request work or information from another.
Checking who a person or service is.
Checking whether that identity may perform this action on this record.
Server-side code that applies rules and manages stored data.
A record of a specified achievement issued under stated assessment rules.
Computers and storage operated remotely and accessed over a network.
An organized store of records that can be queried and updated.
A server record granting an account access to specified learning content.
Work products and observations that support a claim.
The interface a person sees and interacts with.
A repeated request produces one intended effect rather than duplicating it.
A text format for structured data using objects, lists and simple values.
Data saved by a browser for one site on one device.
A small product scope used to test a specific assumption with real users.
A named input whose value controls a calculation or model.
A collection of work with clear context, contribution and evidence.
Instructions and context supplied to a generative model.
Previously working behavior that fails after a change.
Explicit criteria used to assess a piece of work consistently.
An isolated environment for controlled practice or execution.
A definition of expected data fields, types and constraints.
A language used to query and manage relational data.
An HTTP message a service sends when an event occurs.
